intro: A melody of long notes floats above five-note groups in the left hand. Rachmaninoff’s own recording carries that flowing accompaniment through a more unsettled middle passage and back to the opening, before a high decorative close.
question: How does the five-note accompaniment support a melody that moves more slowly?

cues.title: Five notes beneath a long line
cues.text: The left hand groups its moving notes in fives, while the upper melody uses longer values and its own smaller decorations. Follow the upper line without counting every accompaniment note as a new beat.
cues.evidence: Gutheil’s 1911 score, printed p. 22, shows the quintuplet accompaniment beneath longer melodic notes. The report confirms continuous opening activity at a low level; its onset-tempo estimate is not used as a beat measurement.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Rachmaninoff’s first Victor year
cues.text: Rachmaninoff recorded this Prelude in Camden, New Jersey, on 3 May 1920, shortly after signing with Victor. The register identifies the venue as the Church Building Laboratory and the released performance as take one.
cues.evidence: DAHR records C-23985 take 1 on 3 May 1920 at Camden’s Church Bldg. Laboratory: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/700009184/C-23985-Prelude_in_G_major_op._32_no._5. The RCA booklet dates his Victor contract to 21 April 1920.

cues.title: A more unsettled continuation
cues.text: In the middle expansion, listen for the melody changing register while the harmonic setting becomes less stable. The accompaniment’s regular motion provides continuity even when the upper line no longer resembles the opening phrase.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 23–24 changes the line’s register and chromatic setting before the return on p. 24. The report gives a boundary at 0:58 and a level increase from −26 dB at 0:55 to −13.8 at 1:00; the middle-region boundary is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One key in a complete collection
cues.text: This G major Prelude belongs to the thirteen pieces of Op. 32, composed in 1910 and published in 1911. Together with Op. 23 and the early C♯ minor Prelude, they cover all twenty-four major and minor keys.
cues.evidence: IMSLP’s catalogue lists the composition and publication dates, the thirteen keys and the complete-key relationship: https://imslp.org/wiki/13_Preludes,_Op.32_(Rachmaninoff,_Sergei)

cues.title: The opening’s familiar balance
cues.text: The return restores the opening’s balance of a sustained melody and moving five-note groups. Listen for recognition in the relationship between the two hands, not only in a single familiar note.
cues.evidence: Score p. 24 marks a tempo over the return of the opening in G major. A boundary at 2:00 and recovered opening pitch-class profile support the approximate placement; the analysis’s recurrent B-minor labels are not treated as the work’s written key.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A transfer, not a new performance
cues.text: The digital source identifies a 1992 RCA reissue. Its booklet credits Ward Marston for disc-to-DAT transfer, with digital remastering by André Gauthier and Anthony Salvatore; those are later production stages, not a second recording session.
cues.evidence: The Archive item identifies RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2 (1992). Its linked booklet, p. 20, credits Marston, Gauthier as supervisor and Salvatore as engineer; the current file’s connection to that mastering follows the uploader’s stated source.

cues.title: The upper decoration gives way
cues.text: The close carries the motion upwards, then reduces it around a trill and the last quiet chords. Listen beyond the decorative figures to the thinning sound: the moving accompaniment finally yields to a held arrival.
cues.evidence: Score p. 25 closes with high figures, a trill, perdendo and a final G-major chord. The report’s boundary at 2:48 precedes a decline from −25 dB at 2:45 to −39.8 at 2:55, with no detected onsets in the 3:00 window.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The regular motion supports a changing line
transitions.how: The opening phrase grows more active and its melody changes register. The recurring accompaniment preserves a thread of motion while the harmony moves away from the original G-major setting. Rather than cutting off the first section with silence, Rachmaninoff uses continuing small note-values to carry the listener into the more chromatic middle writing.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition pp. 23–24 shows the changing melodic register and increasingly chromatic continuation: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e0/IMSLP105591-PMLP02018-Rachmaninov_-_32_-_13_Preludes_(ed.Gutheil).pdf. The 0:58 boundary and nearby level rise support an approximate middle region.

transitions.title: Chromatic wandering releases the opening phrase
transitions.how: The middle passage moves through a chromatic flourish and a held point, then continues with a quieter dolce phrase. As that continuation settles, a tempo restores the opening melody in G major above its characteristic five-note accompaniment. The same relationship between sustained upper notes and small lower figures provides the link back; the return is a recovery of texture as well as key.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 24 supplies the chromatic run, fermata, dolce continuation and later a tempo return. The 2:00 boundary, low relative level and recovered opening profile locate the return approximately; the preceding flourish is not claimed to fall within the playback span.

transitions.title: The line rises into its final decoration
transitions.how: The returning phrase leads to pp leggiero figures high in the keyboard. The left hand initially keeps its five-note motion while the upper part becomes more decorative. A trill then suspends the line as the accompaniment reduces its activity and the final G-major chord settles. The written perdendo turns the last activity into withdrawal rather than another central climax.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 25 contains pp leggiero, high figures, the trill and perdendo. The 2:32 boundary and high activity at 2:35–2:40 locate the decorated closing region; the stronger 2:48 boundary marks its withdrawal.

fields.note: Victor’s contemporary 1925 catalogue lists this Prelude on record 6261, which DAHR maps to the same C-23985 take 1 as the earlier single-faced 74645. This establishes publication no later than 1925, independently of the 1920 session date, and eligibility under the project’s pre-1926 US recording rule. The exact first-publication day remains unknown. The 1992 booklet retains an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any unidentified new creative contribution to the mastering is independently cleared worldwide.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
